steps.title: You tap “Send”
steps.plain: Your message is cut into small numbered pieces — packets — like posting a long letter as several postcards, each marked “1 of 5”, “2 of 5”, and so on.
steps.tech: Packetisation: the app segments the payload and stamps each segment with source/destination addresses and a sequence number (IP + transport headers).

steps.title: First hop: your router
steps.plain: Every packet leaves through the same front door — your router — which passes it to your internet provider. A slow or badly placed router delays every single packet.
steps.tech: The router performs NAT and forwards packets to the ISP gateway using its routing table; Wi-Fi is only this first local hop.

steps.title: Across the internet
steps.plain: Packets race across many networks, often by different routes. It doesn’t matter if postcard 3 arrives before postcard 2 — the numbers fix the order at the end.
steps.tech: Routers forward by destination IP along independent paths; TCP reorders segments and retransmits any that are lost.

steps.title: The chat service sorts it
steps.plain: The app’s servers receive the packets, rebuild the message, store it safely, and get ready to deliver it — even if your friend is offline right now.
steps.tech: The service reassembles the stream, persists the message, and queues a push notification for the recipient’s device.

steps.title: It lands on their phone
steps.plain: Their phone downloads the packets, rebuilds the message in order, and shows it — usually in well under a second, across several networks you never see.
steps.tech: Delivery is confirmed end-to-end; read receipts and “typing…” indicators travel back the same way as tiny packets of their own.

steps.title: You type an address
steps.plain: A name like a shop sign is easier to remember than a street address. Your browser first has to translate that name into the server’s actual numeric address.
steps.tech: A DNS resolver maps the domain to an IP address, usually from cache; this lookup happens before any page data moves.

steps.title: Your browser asks politely
steps.plain: It opens a secure, encrypted conversation with the server and asks: “Please send me this page.” Nobody in between can read what passes.
steps.tech: A TCP connection plus a TLS handshake establishes encryption, then an HTTP request is sent — modern sites use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.

steps.title: The page travels in packets
steps.plain: The page isn’t one file — it’s text, photos, and code arriving as many packets, then rebuilt in your browser in the right order.
steps.tech: The response is segmented, transferred, and reassembled; assets are often served in parallel from a CDN near you.

steps.title: The server does its work
steps.plain: Behind the scenes the server may check a database, personalise the page, or confirm you’re logged in — all before the packets even start back.
steps.tech: Server-side code (for example PHP) queries a database, renders HTML, and returns it with status codes and headers.

steps.title: Your browser builds the page
steps.plain: It lays out text, loads images, and runs the page’s code. A “slow website” is often slow right here — too much to download or build on a modest phone.
steps.tech: The browser parses HTML into the DOM, applies CSS, executes JavaScript, and paints; heavy assets block first paint.

steps.title: You press “Pay”
steps.plain: Only the details needed for this purchase are sent — and never as plain readable text travelling openly across the internet.
steps.tech: The form submits over HTTPS; reputable checkouts tokenise card data so the merchant never stores the full number.

steps.title: Everything gets sealed
steps.plain: Your device scrambles the details into a code that only the payment service can unscramble. Anyone intercepting it sees nonsense.
steps.tech: TLS encrypts in transit; the gateway exchanges tokens with the card network rather than raw card numbers.

steps.title: A middleman checks the route
steps.plain: A payment gateway verifies the details are well-formed, checks for obvious fraud signals, and routes the request to the right bank.
steps.tech: The gateway calls the acquiring bank → card network → issuing bank, carrying amount, currency, and risk signals.

steps.title: Your bank decides
steps.plain: The bank checks it’s really you (sometimes asking for a one-time code), that funds exist, and that nothing looks unusual — then approves or declines in seconds.
steps.tech: The issuer runs fraud scoring and may trigger 3-D Secure (an OTP/app approval) before returning an authorisation code.

steps.title: Both sides keep the receipt
steps.plain: You get a confirmation and the shop gets paid later in a batch. That reference number is your proof if anything needs tracing.
steps.tech: Authorisation is followed by clearing and settlement; the transaction reference links every record across systems.

steps.title: You attach the file
steps.plain: The file is read from your device and prepared for sending, like putting a thick report into several envelopes that each fit through the mail slot.
steps.tech: The browser reads the file as a byte stream and splits it into chunks (often a few MB each) so a failed chunk can be retried without restarting the upload.

steps.title: It uploads in pieces
steps.plain: Each piece is numbered and sent with a label saying where it is going. If your connection hiccups, only the missing piece needs to be sent again.
steps.tech: Chunks are sent as HTTPS requests; each is checksummed so the server can detect corruption and ask for a resend.

steps.title: Across the internet
steps.plain: The pieces take whatever routes are free at that moment. Your upload speed, often much lower than your download speed, sets how fast this part goes.
steps.tech: Packets are routed independently; throughput is capped by the slowest link, which at home is usually the upstream side of the connection.

steps.title: Storage keeps copies
steps.plain: The service reassembles the file and stores it, usually in more than one place, so one broken disk does not mean a lost file.
steps.tech: The service verifies the whole-file hash, writes to object storage, and replicates it across disks or data centres.

steps.title: Your teacher opens it
steps.plain: When your teacher clicks the link, the same journey runs in reverse: the pieces come down, are put back in order, and the file opens exactly as you saved it.
steps.tech: A download is served from storage, often via a nearby cache; the client checks the size and hash before opening it.
